sources.news_title: Moment OpenAI engineer 'caught looking at spy device he left in top secret room'
sources.text:
OpenAI, the tech giant behind ChatGPT, said it found a hidden recording device tucked into one of its executive conference rooms.
The San Francisco-based AI company said yesterday that staff had to use one of its models to ‘understand the device and where it had come from’.
The bug was slipped behind the TV of a room where high-level chats about confidential plans, government relationships and research happened.
A ‘specific employee had planted it a few days earlier’ in late September, OpenAI said on X, adding that the staffer has since been arrested.
The US Department of Justice named the worker as Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, from Saudi Arabia.
He has been charged with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
Alfozan appeared in court today and remains in custody.
Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan is accused of asking a productivity AI assistant questions about meeting rooms.
They included ‘can you list today’s meeting in this room’, according to the court document.
Prompts – instructions to an AI – to a chatbot used by Alfozan’s spouse included how to build a ‘continuous audio recorder’.
Alfozan was seen on CCTV near the executive conference room ‘on multiple dates’ just before the gadget was planted, the complaint said.
The wiretapping device was stuffed into a USB stick, wrapped in toilet paper and planted behind a TV in the room on September 28, officials said.
OpenAI discovered the spy device two days later.
A photo in the court document shows an object on the back of a TV.
Another image shows the gadget with the branding of Seeed Studio, which makes AI-powered hardware.
Alfozan had no authority to access the meetings in the room but footage allegedly shows him peeking behind the TV and looking at where the recording device had been stashed on October 5.
OpenAI told Metro that the recording device was designed to evade detection and used ‘advanced encryption’, so it would be tough to crack, and could monitor audio and had a way to transfer data without being noticed.
The company also has evidence that the employee intended to deploy other recording devices in top-secret rooms.
After searching a bag left unattended by Alfozan in OpenAI offices, FBI agents discovered a second recording device, according to the indictment.
If convicted, Alfozan faces five years in prison and up to $250,000 (nearly £190,000) in fines.
Alfozan began working at OpenAI in July 2025. Since September last year, he has been an engineering lead, according to a LinkedIn profile bearing his name.
OpenAI fired him on October 9, the day he was arrested. It timed the firing of its employee with the FBI to avoid disrupting the investigation.
The company gradually limited the worker’s access to company systems and offices, then suspended his access, put him on leave and confiscated his work equipment.
Alfozan’s lawyer, William Pernik, told Metro that his client is ‘presumed innocent’.
‘These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why,’ he added.
OpenAI said: ‘At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated.
‘We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.
‘Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.’

An OpenAI engineer was arrested for allegedly planting a covert recording device in a conference room used for confidential executive discussions at the company.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national who worked at OpenAI, was arrested on Oct. 9 and charged with using or attempting to use an electronic device to intercept oral communications. He appeared in federal court on Oct. 13 and remains in custody. According to the U.S. Department of Justice, he is scheduled for a detention hearing on Oct. 19.
“Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” Kash Patel, director of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), said in a statement
The investigation began after OpenAI employees discovered a concealed audio recording device on Sept. 30 in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco office. The device was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television and allegedly concealed with toilet paper.

According to the complaint, the room was reserved for discussions involving highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans and business-development opportunities. It was also used for discussions about nonpublic information concerning OpenAI’s technical progress, strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements and commercial relationships.
According to prosecutors, the device was installed around Sept. 28. Its stored data was encrypted, preventing investigators from immediately accessing the recordings.
Investigators allege that surveillance footage showed Alfozan near the room on several occasions, despite not having permission to access it or attend its meetings. Security footage also showed him looking behind the television where the device had been installed.
“Protecting American SI [super intelligence] innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” Patel added.
The complaint further states that Alfozan used an internal productivity tool to gather information about the office layout, including meeting room schedules and executive movements. Investigators also examined prompts submitted through a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse. The prompts included questions about building and customizing an audio recorder, improving audio quality and live listening, encrypting an SD card, and enabling remote access.

Authorities have not publicly established a motive for the alleged actions.
The investigation also found that on the day he entered the executive conference room, Alfozan allegedly left another recording device inside a bag unattended in a separate room at the office. The bag also contained his wallet and identification.
The incident led OpenAI to terminate Alfozan’s employment and refer the matter to the FBI.
The company said it found no indication that the employee had improperly accessed or extracted its model weights, source code or customer data.
According to Alfozan’s LinkedIn profile, he holds a master’s degree in data science from the University of California, Berkeley. Before joining OpenAI, he worked at Meta as a senior systems engineer and was a founding engineer at Nash.
OpenAI is cooperating with the ongoing investigation. If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and up to three years of supervised release.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation arrested Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi Arabian national and OpenAI engineer, on Friday for reportedly hiding an audio recording device in the company’s San Francisco executive conference room, the Department of Justice announced in a press release Tuesday. The arrest is the latest security incident at OpenAI, whose agents previously breached AI-startup Hugging Face in addition to other outside systems.
“Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence (SI) technology,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in the DOJ’s Tuesday press release, using a new term for AI promoted by the Trump administration. “Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security.”
Alfozan wrapped the recording device in toilet paper, then plugged it into a USB port behind a television in the conference room around Sept. 28, the DOJ said in the release. Security footage showed the OpenAI engineer near the room on several occasions before the device was discovered, even though he was not authorized to enter it. A photo of Alfozan, shared in a post on X, depicts him looking behind the television where the device was placed.

The spokesperson said OpenAI referred the case to the FBI and will keep supporting the bureau’s ongoing probe.
The company’s security team found the encrypted, detection-evading device on Sept. 30 during a sweep of the conference room, according to OpenAI. According to the Justice Department’s October 13 announcement, 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan was arrested on Friday, October 9, and made his initial appearance in federal court on Tuesday.
Alfozan, who had worked as an engineer for OpenAI since July 2025, is accused of placing a concealed recording device in a room where company executives regularly discussed highly confidential information, including proprietary research, advanced AI capabilities, government engagements, and strategic business decisions.
If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine, and three years of supervised release.
According to the DOJ’s press release:
According to the complaint, Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025.
On or about Sept. 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device (Recording Device 1) inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco.
OpenAI determined that the device, which had been concealed in toilet paper, was installed on or about Sept. 28, and that its contents were encrypted.
Recording Device 1
Closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage inside OpenAI’s office showed that Alfozan appeared near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery, although he had no authority to access or to participate in meetings occurring in the executive conference room.
According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where Recording Device 1 was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about Open AI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships.
According to the complaint, prior to Sept. 28, Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about Open AI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, “leadership and exec” locations, and external partner meetings.
Moreover, a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse (which shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s own chatbot account) submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device, including inquiries about “build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,” “customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,” “improv[ing] audio and live listening,” and “encrypt[ing] the SD card,” among other things.
The same chatbot account also submitted prompts specifically related to Recording Device 1, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between Sept. 27 and Sept. 28.
The complaint further alleges that on Oct. 5, Alfozan entered the executive conference room and appeared to look behind the television into which Recording Device 1 had been inserted, as captured below:

Finally, the complaint alleges that, also on or about Oct. 5, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different room in an OpenAI building. OpenAI security personnel found and opened Alfozan’s bag, inside which they discovered — among other things, including Alfozan’s wallet and ID — another recording device (Recording Device 2) similar to Recording Device 1.
FBI Director Kash Patel stated: “According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology. sources.news_title: FBI Arrests OpenAI Employee Suspected of Planting a Surveillance Bug
sources.text:
The FBI arrested an OpenAI employee and charged him with planting a surveillance device in an executive conference room to record the company’s plans for its artificial intelligence, the company and FBI confirmed on Tuesday.
The US Department of Justice identified the employee as 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi Arabian citizen and legal permanent resident of the US, who joined OpenAI’s product team in July 2025. He was fired and arrested on Oct. 9 on suspicion of violating US law by using “an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” The charge comes with a possible five-year prison sentence and a $250,000 fine.
In a statement, Jay Clayton, director of national intelligence, said that the incident underscores the importance of US success in AI development as “a national security prerogative.”
More from CNET
The complaint, filed in the Northern District of California, says Alfozan allegedly placed a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and microSD storage.” It was wrapped in toilet paper and stuck into a TV port. A second recording device was found in a bag Alfozan allegedly left in a printer room along with his wallet and ID.
The conference room where he allegedly planted the bug could be reserved only by executives and their assistants — Alfozan did not have access — and was frequently used to discuss proprietary research and hold meetings with government and industry officials. OpenAI said it has evidence Alfozan planned to place additional surveillance bugs to secretly record company meetings.
The ChatGPT maker says it discovered the first bug on Sept. 30 and alerted the FBI. During the 10 days between the discovery and arrest, the company says it took steps to contain the security risk. The company says it has not seen evidence that the safety of its products or customer data has been compromised.
“We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance,” OpenAI said in a statement.
(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)
AI and national security
OpenAI’s own AI was used to analyze forensic images of the device and assess changes in its data. In a bizarre detail that borders on a marketing pitch, OpenAI posted on X that its frontier AI was used to help investigators. There are no additional details on how its AI was used, but we may learn more later, as the investigation is ongoing.
This incident is one of the first public instances of an espionage case against an AI lab. In 2024, former Google engineer Linwei Ding was found guilty of stealing the company’s AI plans for Chinese rivals, though his conviction was partially overturned in August.
In the intense, cash-fueled worldwide competition to make the most advanced AI, a case of apparent industrial espionage isn’t surprising. What is noteworthy is how the government is responding: Washington is continuing its campaign to ensure that AI companies are seen as critical national infrastructure.
“Protecting American [super intelligence] innovation is critically important, and FBI views it as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in an X post.
The federal government has become more involved with AI policy and with the labs creating the tech in recent months. The US’ voluntary, largely ceremonial AI Accord announced this month had many Big Tech leaders agreeing to develop AI responsibly in the wake of renewed public concern triggered in part by multiple incidents of AI agents breaking into places they shouldn’t have been able to access.
President Trump has consistently championed an “innovation first” strategy to ensure the US beats China, at the expense of AI regulation. His administration has highlighted “national security considerations” that come with AI. The Department of Defense has previously sided with AI labs, saying in a filing in a lawsuit brought by Memphis communities against Elon Musk’s xAI that the data centers powering AI are essential to military and national security activities.

The Briefing:
- Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national who was a member of OpenAI's product team since July 2025, was arrested on Friday, October 9, and charged with using an electronic device to intercept oral communications.
- An audio recorder hidden in a USB port on the rear of a conference room television was found on September 30; prosecutors say it was installed two days earlier and its stored contents were encrypted.
- A chatbot account linked to Alfozan's spouse submitted research queries on building audio recorders in the days before installation; a second device was later found in an unattended bag alongside Alfozan's wallet and ID.
- Senior U.S. officials — including FBI Director Kash Patel and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton — publicly framed the arrest as a national security matter tied to the global competition over artificial intelligence supremacy.
- If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine, and three years of supervised release; a detention hearing is set for October 19.
An encrypted audio recorder concealed in a USB port on the rear of a conference room television sat inside one of OpenAI's San Francisco buildings for approximately 48 hours before company personnel found it and called the FBI. What began as an internal security discovery has since become a federal counterintelligence case with the Director of National Intelligence speaking about it publicly — a sign of how seriously the U.S. government is treating a threat it believes goes beyond one engineer and one company.
The Executive Suite at the Center of the Alleged Scheme
The conference room where the device was found is not a general meeting space. Prosecutors say it is where senior OpenAI executives regularly convene to discuss proprietary research, product roadmaps, commercial relationships, government engagements, and the company's broader technological strategy — exactly the category of information a competitor or foreign intelligence operation would most want to obtain.
The recording device was installed on or about September 28 and was wrapped in toilet paper to conceal it within the USB port. OpenAI security personnel discovered it two days later on September 30. The company established that whatever audio the device captured had been encrypted, suggesting the material was built to travel somewhere securely.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national who had been part of OpenAI's product team since joining the company in July 2025, is the person federal prosecutors say put it there. A YouTube video shared last month had reportedly described him as the only Saudi national employed at OpenAI at the time.
A Digital Trail of Preparation
Before installing anything physical, Alfozan allegedly assembled information. According to the complaint unsealed on October 13, he used an internal company productivity tool in the days before September 28 to query OpenAI's systems for building addresses, conference room capacities and schedules, the locations of executive personnel, and the timing of meetings involving outside partners. Prosecutors describe these searches as methodical groundwork consistent with planning where and when to place a surveillance device.
The chatbot evidence adds a second layer. A chatbot account linked to Alfozan's spouse — one that shared technical identifiers with Alfozan's own account — submitted a series of prompts between September 24 and September 30 covering how to build and customize a continuous audio recorder, extend wireless connectivity, improve live audio capture, and encrypt an SD card. On September 27, and again on the day of the alleged installation, September 28, that same account ran queries referencing the specific device's unique MAC address and custom header. Closed-circuit footage from inside the building also captured Alfozan approaching the executive conference room on multiple dates before the device's discovery, even though he had no authorization to enter the space or attend any meeting held there.
The Second Device and the Arrest
The case against Alfozan hardened significantly on October 5. Footage obtained by prosecutors shows him entering the executive conference room that day and appearing to examine the area behind the television — the exact location from which the first device had been removed. Later that same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in another part of the building. When OpenAI security personnel opened it, they found a second recording device nearly identical to the first, resting next to his wallet and a piece of government-issued identification.
Alfozan was arrested four days later, on Friday, October 9. OpenAI terminated his employment on the same day. In its public statement on October 13, the company said it had used its own AI models to analyze the recovered device, determine its origins, and trace it to the employee who had planted it. OpenAI also disclosed that it possesses evidence indicating Alfozan intended to plant additional recording devices in other restricted areas of the company.
How the U.S. Government Characterized the Threat
The official response from Washington made clear this was not being handled as an ordinary corporate security breach. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton stated that the case demonstrated why prevailing in the global superintelligence competition is a national security imperative, and he credited President Trump's creation of the Super Intelligence Force through National Security Presidential Memorandum 11 as central to that effort.
FBI Director Kash Patel described the alleged plot as an attempt to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's superintelligence technology, and said that defending American AI innovation is "one of our highest counterintelligence priorities." U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California was equally direct: "For us it is a matter of national security," he said, framing the prosecution as part of an ongoing commitment to protecting American technological leadership in the AI era.
What the Complaint Does Not Allege
Despite the national security framing, the federal complaint stops short of connecting the alleged scheme to any foreign government. Prosecutors have not alleged that Alfozan acted at the direction of Saudi Arabia or any other state actor, have not identified a foreign handler, and have not established that the recordings — if any audio was ever captured — were transmitted to any outside party. The FBI investigation is ongoing.
What Comes Next in Court
Alfozan made his initial federal court appearance on October 13, the day prosecutors unsealed the complaint. He remained in federal custody as of that date. A detention hearing is scheduled for October 19. Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Parker for the Northern District of California is leading the prosecution, with support from Trial Attorney Kate Tagert of the National Security Division's Counterintelligence and Export Control Section. Neither Alfozan nor any legal representative acting on his behalf had issued a public response to the charges as of this report.

sources.text:
An OpenAI engineer has been arrested and charged with planting a hidden audio recorder in a conference room used by the company's executives at its San Francisco headquarters, federal prosecutors said Tuesday, in a case the company says it cracked partly with its own AI models. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national who joined OpenAI's product team in July 2025, was taken into custody by the FBI on Oct. 9 and fired the same day. He is charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications, which carries up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
According to the criminal complaint, OpenAI staff found the device at the end of September, concealed behind a television in an executive conference room reserved for highly confidential meetings. Prosecutors described it as a sophisticated, encrypted recorder, wrapped in toilet paper to hide it. Alfozan was not authorized to enter the room, the Justice Department said, but security footage showed him near it on multiple occasions before the device was discovered. On Oct. 5, OpenAI security found a bag he had left unattended in another company building; inside were his wallet, his identification and a second recording device similar to the first.
Investigators said Alfozan had searched for information about OpenAI's buildings, meeting rooms, calendars, the locations of executives and meetings with outside partners. A ChatGPT account, prosecutors said, had submitted prompts containing details that matched the device later recovered from the conference room. OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its internal models to identify the person responsible and to trace the device's origins, found evidence that he intended to place additional recorders in sensitive areas of its offices, and referred the matter to the FBI, which is continuing to investigate.
"Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology," FBI Director Kash Patel said. Neither the complaint nor the company has said what Alfozan intended to do with any recordings, whether anyone else was involved, or whether he was acting for a third party. The charge is a wiretap offense, not espionage or theft of trade secrets, and no foreign government has been named in connection with the case. Alfozan has not entered a plea, and no attorney was listed for him in court records on Tuesday.
The case lands on a company that has become one of the most closely guarded in American industry. OpenAI's executive meetings concern model capabilities, compute contracts, government relationships and the company's own restructuring, and its San Francisco offices have been locked down before — last year over a threat from an activist, and routinely for visits by officials. The arrest of an insider with a recorder behind the television is a different kind of breach, one that physical security against outsiders does not address, and it will be read across an industry whose competitive advantage lives in conversations as much as in code.
It also lands on a company whose relationships with Saudi Arabia are a matter of public record. OpenAI has courted Gulf investment and has discussed data-center projects in the region; Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund and its AI ambitions have made the kingdom a sought-after partner for American AI firms. Nothing in the complaint connects Alfozan's nationality to his alleged conduct, and prosecutors did not suggest a state link. But the detail was in the Justice Department's first sentence, and the question of who, if anyone, wanted to hear what OpenAI's executives say to one another is the one the FBI's continuing investigation is presumably asking.
OpenAI's own account of how it caught him is the part of the story the company chose to tell. Using internal models to comb access logs, footage and search histories is the kind of security application the company has described in general terms as a use case for its systems; the arrest gives it a concrete example, at some cost to the image of a workplace where such tools are necessary. The company said it found the device, identified the employee, established his intent and brought in the FBI — a sequence that took roughly a week and a half from discovery to arrest.
What happens next is a federal prosecution of a single wiretap count, which could be resolved quickly or could expand if the investigation establishes that the recorder captured anything, that the recordings went anywhere, or that Alfozan was not acting alone. The company has said it has evidence of a broader plan; the complaint describes a second device and a search history. Whether that adds up to a man who wanted to know what his bosses thought of him or something more will determine whether this remains a strange episode at one company or becomes the first prosecuted case of its kind in an industry that has been warning about exactly this.

Washington, Oct 14 (SocialNews.XYZ) A Saudi Arabian engineer working for OpenAI has been arrested on federal charges of allegedly installing a concealed audio recording device inside an executive conference room at the artificial intelligence company's San Francisco offices, US authorities announced on Tuesday (local time).
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was arrested on October 9 and made his first appearance in federal court on October 13, according to the Justice Department.
Federal prosecutors charged him with using or attempting to use an electronic device to intercept oral communications. He faces a maximum prison sentence of five years and a fine of $250,000 if convicted.
The case has raised national security concerns in Washington because the conference room was used for discussions involving sensitive research, proprietary technology, business strategy and government engagements.
On September 30, company personnel discovered a concealed recording device inserted into a USB port behind a television in an executive conference room.
Investigators said the device, wrapped in toilet paper to conceal it, had apparently been installed around September 28. Its contents were encrypted.
The complaint alleges that surveillance footage showed Alfozan near the conference room on several occasions, although he was not authorised to access the room or participate in meetings held there.
Prosecutors said the room was regularly used for confidential discussions involving technical developments, commercial opportunities, product plans and the company's relationships with government agencies and business partners.
Investigators also examined digital activity allegedly associated with Alfozan.
According to the complaint, he had used a productivity tool to search for information about OpenAI buildings, meeting rooms, executive locations and external partner meetings.
A chatbot account associated with his spouse, which investigators said shared several identifiers with Alfozan's account, had submitted queries about constructing, installing and concealing recording equipment.
The queries also concerned wireless connectivity, remote listening and encryption.
Federal authorities said the account had made inquiries specifically related to the device found inside the conference room.
On October 5, surveillance footage allegedly showed Alfozan entering the executive conference room and looking behind the television where the first recording device had been discovered.
That same day, OpenAI security personnel found another similar recording device inside a bag that Alfozan had left unattended elsewhere in the building, according to prosecutors.
FBI Director Kash Patel said the investigation involved protecting sensitive American technology.
"Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation's economic strength and national security," Patel said, referring to super intelligence technology.
US Attorney Craig Missakian for the Northern District of California said the case highlighted the importance of protecting technological innovation.
"For us it is a matter of national security," he said.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also linked the case to Washington's efforts to maintain American leadership in advanced artificial intelligence.
The Justice Department said the prosecution supports a national security presidential memorandum intended to protect American advances in super intelligence technology.
Authorities have not publicly established that information collected through the alleged recording device was transmitted to a foreign government. The complaint also does not establish that the Saudi government directed or participated in the alleged conduct.
